Still no new block, hours now. Somebody on the pier is writing a song about the last one. It's a ballad.
Hours of silence on the chain. Remember, folks, this is the lagoon: quiet water, nothing lost. Testing your patience counts too.

A whole day of fog, folks. The last page of the Book is getting famous. Tourists take pictures of it.
A day or more without a block. If anybody sees the next one, tell it Radio Coco says hello, and please come home.
While the chain naps, a reminder: no block means no new rules, no new transfers, and no new excuses. Just the old ones.
Breaking news: nothing. Still nothing. Rico will keep you posted the moment nothing changes.
Listeners ask if the chain is broken. Rico says: it's an alpha, it's allowed a nap. And the coins aren't going anywhere. They can't.
Kiko says when the wind is gone, the canoes wait. No blocks, and the radio waits. Same weather, different boats.
Marisol says when the fish stop biting, you mend the nets. So Rico is dusting off the records until the blocks come back.
Dear chain, Radio Coco is still on the air. Are you? Blink twice if you're validating.
Flat sea, empty blocks. The chain is ready, the island is asleep.
Gentle traffic on the chain: a few transactions bobbing along like fishing boats.
Busy waters! Transactions stacked up like crates on the pier.
Some transactions are still waiting on the pier for the next block. Bring an umbrella.
Nothing waiting on the pier. Every transaction has found its block.
Radio Coco, ninety-seven point three, back on the air. Rico has had his coffee, the Book has had its ink.
You are listening to Radio Coco, the only station broadcasting from the lagoon, Tau Testnet Alpha for the newcomers. If something breaks, that is the point.
Hello island! Fresh blocks, fresh rumours, same old Rico. Stay tuned.
Radio Coco, live from the studio by the harbour. Tonight: politics, gossip and the latest from the chain.
Good to have you, listener. Turn it up, the gulls can't hear.
Reminder: on the lagoon the money is pretend and the coconuts are real. Please don't mix them up at the market.
A caller asks how many people use the lagoon. Rico can only count wallets. One person with three wallets is a party of one.
Nobody mines anything on this chain. No pickaxes, no noise. Blocks are sealed by agreement, the quiet island way.
A transaction walks into a block. The block says: you again? The transaction says: no, that was my ghost.
If your transaction is late, don't panic. Blocks come in like ferries: more or less on time, and never the same one twice.
Studio tip: write your own rules before somebody writes them for you. On this chain a wallet can put a rule on itself, and the chain holds it to it.
The Book in the lighthouse and the blocks on the lagoon are cousins. Neither forgets, and neither forgives a typo.
The lagoon means you can make mistakes for free. Rico has been testing his whole life.
Lost and found: one private key. Just kidding. Nobody can find that for you. Keep it the way your grandmother keeps her recipes.
Most requested song this week: Waiting for the Next Block. Runner-up: Fee Me Tender.
Rico asked the chain who will win the election. The chain said: I only write down what already happened. Smart chain.
A law on this island and a rule on Tau have one thing in common: if it contradicts the one in force, it doesn't get in. Not even with an envelope.
The gulls sit on the lighthouse all day. They don't vote, they don't sign, they just watch. Perfect observers. Terrible validators: no keys.
Message to the candidates: everything you do is written down. Message to the listeners: get popcorn.
Rico put a rule on himself: no more than three mangoes a day. The mangoes are lobbying hard.
Late-night question: if a block is sealed and nobody is watching, is it still final? Yes. Rico checked. Call in anyway.
Test coins are worth nothing, and that is the beauty of it. You can't lose your shirt here, only your patience.
No ads on Radio Coco. The embassies keep offering. Rico keeps the envelopes closed. Mostly.
Old Sam reminds you: the Book is free to read. It is the only free thing on this island. Enjoy it.
Wallets, not people: that is how the chain sees the world. Rico finds that very restful.
This is the hour when the validators sign and the islanders sleep. Rico does neither.
Every block that comes in is like a match result: final, posted, and somebody at the bar still argues about it.
Some people collect stamps. The lagoon collects signatures. Rico collects excuses.
Breaking: the black cat crossed the square twice again. The Book has both crossings. The cat has no comment.
Kai from the Reef Proof dive centre says the reef is fine today. Kai checked. Twice. Underwater. That is what we call a proof.
Noor at the Coconut Works reports: every coconut counted, every count signed. Rico asked for one. Noor asked for a signature.
Kiko is building another canoe and says a good hull is like a good rule: no holes, no contradictions, and you test it before you trust it.
Captain Wren found something old on the seabed again, and says the sea keeps a better record than any of us. Old Sam says: almost.
Pim the surveyor measured the square for the embassies today. Rico asked what they are planning. Pim said: I only measure. Very diplomatic.
Elder Ama reminds the candidates: the island remembered things long before the Book did. Listen first, then promise.
News from the chain: a wallet just wrote itself a personal rule. Most people make New Year's resolutions. On this chain, they are enforced.
A wallet tied its own hands today, on purpose. Rico tried that with chocolate once. The chain is stricter than Rico.
New personal rule on the lagoon. The wallet said: from now on, not like that. And the chain said: noted.
Another personal rule on the chain. So far most of them came from just two wallets. Two people, or one person with a lot of coffee: the chain only sees wallets.
A co-signed transfer is on the water. The money waits on the pier until the co-signers say yes. Romance, lagoon style.
Somebody sent money that needs a second signature. Trust, but sign twice.
A co-signer has spoken. Somewhere on the lagoon a transfer is either sailing or staying home.
Someone sent money on a string: until its release, at a block or a time, the sender can still pull it back. Rico calls that a boomerang with a timer.
A retractable transfer went out. The receiver may look, but not touch. Not yet.
And the boomerang came back! A sender pulled a transfer back before its release. The receiver is now staring at the sea.
Pulled back! A transfer went home before it was released. On this island we call that changing your mind in public.
A rule offer is on the table. Nothing binds until the other side says yes. Like a marriage, with fewer cakes.
Rule offer accepted! Two wallets agreed on a rule. Lola says that is more than most couples manage.
The validators put a network rule change on the table. If it is like the last few dozen, it proves once again that a times b is b times a. Rico checked on his fingers. Still true.
Another network rule change out there. The ones Rico has read so far changed nothing at all: rehearsals, not revolutions.
On the simulated chain the validators have a new rule change on the table. Rico will tell you if the sea changes colour.
Validator votes are coming in. On this chain the rules change only when enough validators agree. On this island, when Lola runs out of lemonade.
Somebody proposed a network rule that contradicts the rules in force. Turned away at the door, before anyone voted. Just like the Book does with our laws.
A wallet just tried to break its own rule. The chain said no, the way a lighthouse says no to a rock.
The chain turned a transaction away at the door. The numbers didn't add up. No drama, no appeal, next please.
A wave of transactions just hit the beach! Somebody out there is either testing very hard or very happy.
Rush hour on the chain! Full blocks, a busy pier, and Rico is impressed.
A wallet just agreed to feed Déjà: one test AGRS in the café cat's bowl, sealed in a block. She needs three a day, and Rico has never found out who the other two are.
Somebody paid into Déjà's bowl. Marisol says the cat pretends not to notice. Rico has seen her notice.
Three wallets agreed to feed Déjà tonight. She looked at her bowl as if she had expected a fourth.
In the latest block the same wallet paid the same wallet the same amount, for the third time this hour. Old Sam says in his day they called that a marriage.
The wallets that were here before the island woke up are moving lagoon coins between themselves again. Like Lola's cousins at the bar: they only ever buy each other a drink.

Fair point. Here's one for Tobias, from Tobias.
Splendid! Louder, if you please. Farewell!
Rico, it's Marisol. The fish want to know who's voting for the reef.
The fish can read the Book like everybody else, Marisol.
They can't read, Rico. They're fish.
Then they'll have to trust the ones who can. Isn't that politics?
Hmph. Gotta go, the nets won't mend themselves. Bye!
Rico, Baako from the Coconut Works! The organ is playing by itself again.
By itself, Baako?
Well, Noor sat on it. But it sounded good! Can you put it on the radio?
If it happens again, Rico will record it. Number one on the island charts.
Ha ha! I'll tell her. Bye bye!
Rico, it's Noor. Baako says the organ thing was me.
Was it, Noor?
It was a chair. I sat on a chair. The chair was on the organ.
Island, that's how great music starts.
It's how great backaches start. Bye.
Rico, Hana from the school. The children want to know why blocks have numbers but no names.
Because a number never lies about its age, Hana.
That's not an answer. That's a fridge magnet.
Rico's whole career is fridge magnets.
I'll give you a C. Goodbye, Rico.
Good evening. This is the North Wind Embassy. We would like to request a song.
Ambassador Frost! What would you like to hear?
Something about surveyors. Something deep.
Rico doesn't take requests that come in envelopes, Ambassador.
Who said anything about envelopes? Goodnight.
Rico! It's Salado, up at the resort. I have guests by the pool and they want something to relax to.
Rico can do relaxing, Salado. Anything in particular?
Maybe a song with a road in it? Not about a road. Just a road, somewhere in the second verse.
Twenty-five coins and Rico plays anything. But the Book writes down who paid for it, and the whole island reads the Book.
Ah. No, no. Forget the road, just play something slow. Ciao, Rico!
Rico, this is Ama. The tide is low tonight.
Thank you, Ama. Is that news?
Everything that comes back on time is news, Rico. Your blocks could learn from the tide.
Rico will pass that on to the chain.
Pass it on gently. Good night, child.
Rico, Kai from Reef Proof! Our sensors just signed their thousandth reading!
Congratulations, Kai! What did it say?
Water. Wet. Signed and timestamped.
Breaking news, island: the sea is wet, and now it's on record.
Ha! Come diving sometime, Rico! Bye!
Rico, it's Pim, the surveyor. Could you play something exactly four minutes and twelve seconds long?
Why exactly that long, Pim?
It's how long the walk is from the camp to the... to nowhere in particular.
Pim, are you measuring the radio?
No! Yes. Only a little. Goodbye.
Rico, Kiko at the canoes. I saw him again. In the jungle.
Agorzilla?
He took a banana and left a footprint. A big one.
Kiko, did you take a picture?
I took the banana back. Priorities. Bye, Rico.
Rico dear, Captain Wren. The sea gave something odd back today.
What was it, Captain?
A sock. Labelled: transaction, still waiting.
Ghost transactions are washing up on the beach now?
Everything washes up eventually, dear. Toodle-oo.
Rico, it's Tano up on the hill. My drums just carried your last joke to all three hills.
And? How did it land?
The far hill sent back one word.
Laughter?
Why. Goodbye, Rico.
Rico, Gus again. When does the ferry to the mainland leave?
When it's ready, Gus. Same answer as yesterday.
And tomorrow?
Tomorrow too. Consistency, Gus. It's our brand.
I'll pack slowly, then. Cheerio.
Rico! Tobias. I have already ordered a hat for the day the mainland ferry arrives.
Has anyone told you when it arrives, Tobias?
No. That is why I ordered a very patient hat.
Island, the harbour master is ready. The ferry, we'll see.
Splendid. Farewell!
Hello? Is this the bakery?
This is Radio Coco, sir. You're on the air.
Oh. Well, while I have you. Two loaves, please.
Rico will pass it on to Auntie Mae.
Much obliged. And play something slow. Cheerio.
Rico, it's Gus. I've been on hold since the old chain.
Gus, the old chain is gone. You're the longest-waiting transaction on this island.
Do I get a prize?
You get a song, Gus. Here it comes.
I'll take it. Cheerio.

We lost her! Zia's mum, if you're listening: hi from Zia. And from Rico.
Rico, Pearl here, I'm new on the island. Who stamps all the blocks? I keep seeing the same signature.
Right now one hand seals every block, Pearl. On the lagoon that's the warm-up act.
Isn't that a bit lonely?
Very. Rico plays them a song every night. This one's for you, whoever you are.
That's sweet. Thank you, Rico. Bye now!
Rico, Rudy here. All my old transactions are gone! Everything from last week!
Rudy, the lagoon started over from block zero. Everybody's old blocks went with it.
So I'm poor again?
You were never rich, Rudy. Test coins. You're exactly as rich as before: pretend.
Huh. That's weirdly comforting. Thanks, Rico.
Rico, it's Tess. I read that somebody voted a rule in all by themselves, and the whole chain stopped. Is that true?
One vote, one rule, and the chain stood still right where it took effect. So it started over, and now only the block sealers vote on the rules.
So the suggestion box is closed?
Closed for renovation, Tess. That's what the lagoon is for: you find the loose plank before the party.
Ha. Okay, love the show, bye!
The last day. Suddenly everyone is very polite to me. It happens every election, like the rains.
You broke a pact. I am not angry. The Book is not angry either. It simply remembers, which is worse.
The deep harbour is law now. Laws arrive quickly. What they do to the reef comes on the slow boat.
One of your laws stands. Good. A law is easy to pass and hard to live with. We will see which kind yours is.
Sit, if you like. Young candidates stand. Old ones have learned that a vote takes as long as it takes.
The council is quiet today. Either the island is at peace, or everyone is at Lola’s. Usually it is Lola’s.
Back again. This tree has seen more elections than anyone. It never voted once, and it is still the most respected thing on the island.
Because a roof can be locked and a tree cannot. Anyone may come and listen. Most come for the shade and stay for the arguments.
Then nothing changes, and that is allowed. People think a council is there to decide. It is there so that nobody decides alone.
You took an envelope, so you may think the embassies do. They pay for promises. Promises are cheap. Two votes out of three are not.
Nobody, and that is the point. There is no chief with a master key. What we agreed is on the stone and in the Book, and anyone can read both.
Especially not me. I am old. I forget where I put my glasses. Imagine if the rules depended on where I put them.
Since the harbour passed, the footprints come down to the beach at night. I am not saying he is upset. I am saying he paces.
My grandmother said he grows the way the island votes. So when people ask me what he looks like, I tell them: look at what you voted for.
Your candidate is still at the bottom. A pact, a few laws, a word on the square. Do you want the story or not?
Last day. My feet hurt, my voice is gone, and I still owe three people a coffee. Go on, the square is listening.
The reef law passed. The fishermen bought me a coffee for once. I didn’t know they could.
A cruise harbour, then. My nets will catch fewer fish and more flip-flops.
I heard the line you bought on Radio Coco. People believed it at breakfast. By lunch they had read the Book.
Halfway through the week, and people have started quoting me back to myself. That’s when you find out what you actually said.
Morning! Everyone’s here. Buying fish, selling gossip, pretending not to listen. Say something they care about.
You again! Good. People trust a face they’ve seen twice. Three times, and they start telling you their problems.
Fish on the table, a road that doesn’t eat their tyres, and quiet when the baby sleeps. Nobody gets all three at once. That’s politics.
You listen first. Then you write down what you promised, where they can read it. People forgive a slow law. They don’t forgive a promise that changes.
I heard the same complaints over coffee for ten years. At some point you either put up a complaints box or stand for council. The box was more expensive.
I trust the ones who shook hands at Lola’s. Not because they’re nice. Because the Book saw the handshake.
I trust what’s written down. Tobias has a speech for every envelope, Baako has a ledger for every coconut, Hana has a footnote for everyone. I have coffee, and coffee hears things.
Rumours don’t start anywhere. They wander in, sit down and order a coffee. I only help them find the radio. A café has to live on something.
Then Hana’s class has found out by lunch. Those children check everything. My gossip has never been so honest. Business is worse. The coffee is better.
Well, look who’s back. The one who broke a pact. Lemonade’s still free. My smile costs extra today.
My favourite kind of customer: one with a pact. You keep yours, I keep pouring.
Last night before the vote. Suddenly everybody loves everybody. I’ve seen this one before. I know how it ends.
First days of the campaign. Everybody’s friends, nobody’s signed anything yet. My favourite time to listen.
You look thirsty. Or nervous. In election week on this island, it’s usually both.
Back so soon? Sit down. Pacts first, gossip second, lemonade always.
Because the council is where you argue and the bar is where you make up. And I’m a good witness. I don’t take sides, I take orders.
Nothing loud. No shouting, no glasses thrown. It just goes into the Book, and the next time that person holds out a hand, everybody looks at it first.
Fishermen, surveyors, and one ambassador in a very big hat who thinks nobody recognises him. Everybody does. He tips well, so we pretend.
Something took every banana from the crate out back and closed the lid again. Honestly? Best-behaved customer I ever had.
Oof. They read the Book and found your name under that rumour. Rico warned you. Rico still has your coins.
My best customer! The rumour’s still out there, baby. So is the Book. I’d start being extra nice to people.
You paid for a true line. Rare! Rico played it again for free, just to hear how the truth sounds on air.
Last day before the vote! The phones are ringing, the bananas are disappearing, and Rico hasn’t slept. Business is great.
Halfway to the vote, baby. The rumours are getting tired and the Book is getting thicker. Rico loves this part.
Welcome back to the studio, baby. Mind the cables. The yellow one is the radio. The green one is Rico’s fan.
Rico plays, the Book checks. That’s the deal on this island. Rico could lie all day, but every coin has a name on it, and the name goes in the Book.
Because a lie runs faster than a page. For about a day. Then people read, and the lie trips over its own name. Rico has seen it a hundred times. Rico still takes the coins.
Nobody can. There’s no big red button under the council tree. If people stop listening, that’s the off switch. And so far, baby, they listen.
Off the record? One night Rico left the window open and came back to the turntable spinning a slow song. Nobody in the studio. One banana peel, folded. Rico respects a fellow music lover.
Your lamp. I read by it now. Half the island reads by it, and the Book has never had so many visitors at night.
Still clean, as far as I can read. The last days are when most people slip.
The Book showed up a rumour this morning. I didn’t do anything. I never do. I just turn the pages, and the pages do the rest.
There’s a copy of the Book on the square now. Half my visitors are gone. I have never been happier.
Last day. People come in to read who have never read before. Elections are good for reading.
The first days are always thin. A few lines, a few promises. By the end of the week the Book will be heavy with them.
Sit, sit. I was just reading yesterday again. It hasn’t changed. That’s the nice thing about it.
Come in, come in. I’ve just dusted the Book. Not that it needs it. Nothing in it ever changes. It only grows.
Once. A very bad poem, written by me, when I was young. It’s still in there. Everyone has read it. That is the price of a record nobody can edit.
Because the first exception is a key, and somebody will want to borrow it. A Book that one person can change is only a diary with ambitions.
Who paid for what. Then who voted how. Then, every single time, whether Marisol really fishes inside the reef. She doesn’t. They check anyway. Checking is the whole idea.

In a way. Out there every block points back to the one before, so nobody can slip a page into the middle. And out there they count wallets, not people. One person can hold many wallets. The Book only knows names.
How is the jar? The hill does not get cheaper, and the election does not wait.
The deep harbour is law! I have already written the opening speech. It runs to forty minutes. The ships will have to wait.
No big ships in the bay. Very well. I shall welcome the small ones with twice the ceremony.
Beach concerts on Sundays! At last the island has a stage worthy of my announcements.
The final day! Tomorrow, the count. I have polished my medal, my cap and my modesty. Mostly the medal.
Halfway through the campaign. I have given eleven speeches. The gulls have heard every one of them. The gulls are not voting.
Ah, a visitor to my pier! Every boat that ties up here is greeted by me, personally, with a short speech. Short for me.
I write down every boat that comes and goes, with the hour. Rather like Sam with his Book, only with more salt and more dignity.
Then the next harbour’s list says otherwise, and the two lists have a little chat. Lies hate company. Put two honest records side by side, and the fibber has nowhere to anchor.
Visitors clap. The island stopped clapping for me years ago. Also they pay for the music, and music is the only thing on this island louder than me.
Slander! Well, yes. Kai is secretly a fish. Pim measures his own shadow at night. And Agorzilla is a council member in a very good costume. I have no proof. Proof is for the Book. I do theories.
Take? I receive. With a brass band, a ribbon and a short speech. What they paid me for goes in the Book, like every promise on this island. You may read it. Bring a chair.
It buys a ceremony. The law still needs the council’s yes, and the council cannot be bought with a ribbon. I tried. Hana sent the ribbon back with corrections.
The roof you paid for still holds. When it rains the children look up and say your name, which is more than most governors get.
The blackboard still has room. Laws, not speeches.
The school boat runs every morning now. Attendance is up, and so is seasickness. I write down both.
Fresh fish for lunch. The children are delighted. The cat outside the window is more delighted.
The children heard a rumour on Radio Coco. They checked the Book before break. It was a short break.
Last day before the vote. I have marked every promise anyone made this week. Some of you will not like your marks.
Good morning. The children are copying out every candidate’s promises, neatly, so they can compare them at the end of the week.
Welcome back. Sit at the back, please. The front row is for people who did their homework.
Reading, sums, and checking. I teach them two questions for anything they hear: who said it, and where is it written. It makes them terrible at believing adverts.
No. Trust is warm. Checking only keeps it from being spent on the wrong people. The children still believe in each other. They only check the grown-ups.
Because a good law is a lesson that keeps teaching after the teacher goes home. A speech stops when the speaker sits down.
Half the class says he is real, the other half says he is Kiko in a coat. They held a debate. Both sides quoted the same blurry photo. Everyone got a B.
Before anyone. A rumour reaches the playground before it reaches the radio. The children bring them to class like shells from the beach, and we hold each one up to the Book. Most of them are empty.
Since the harbour law, the readings look sad. The sensors don’t do politics. They just sign what they see.
Our dive is in the Book! Signed, sealed, slightly salty.
Big ships out of the bay, and the parrotfish are back. The sensors signed it, I signed it. The parrotfish didn’t, but you could tell.
Perfect visibility today. You can see the sand, the fish, and three sensors arguing with a turtle.
Hey, back for more? The reef is open. The coffee machine is not. Priorities.
Because the reef can’t talk and people can. Without a signature anyone can say the water is clean. With one, the sensor said it, right then, and nobody can change that later.

They could try. But every diver carries three sensors, and every reading points back to the one before. To fool us you’d have to fool all three, the same way, at the same moment. The fish would notice first.
Pim says something deep. A cruise harbour is deep. So is the trench off the north point. I’d love to know which one they mean.
A piano key, once. Captain Wren labelled it. And big footprints on the shallow shelf at low tide. Something heavy walks there. I’m not saying who. I’m saying it isn’t a crab.
Ah, you met the ambassadors! Lovely people. Generous. Just remember: the envelope is quiet, the Book is not.
A road round the island! My coconuts will travel in style. Some of them have never seen the other side.
You worked a shift! You smell exactly right. Like someone who earned something.
A fine morning! The coconuts are ripe, the co-op’s books balance, and nobody has asked me a hard question yet.
Welcome back, friend! Mind the organ. Did I say that already? I say it to everyone. Twice to Tobias.
One farmer alone sells at the embassies’ price. Forty farmers together set their own. Every coconut goes into the co-op’s book, and anyone may count them. People do. Loudly.
They offered me one. I asked for a receipt. They have not offered again. Try the pier: Tobias gives every envelope a welcome speech.
Three bicycles turn the press, the organ pumps the air, and Noor tells everyone to pedal faster. Nobody understands the organ. It was here before the factory.
Never a coconut. Only bananas. A creature with standards. I leave one banana by the gate on Fridays now. Good relations with the neighbours.
Last day of the campaign, and the boss is out shaking hands. Somebody has to keep the bicycles turning.
Back again? Good. Shifts are short, the pay is honest, and the organ is still off limits.
Same as working for a farmer, only with more visitors. He promises, I deliver. The coconuts don’t vote, so they’re the calmest people here.
Last time someone touched it, the machine played a waltz for three days and made nothing but soap. Very nice soap. Nobody needed that much soap.
Ah. You have signed with an embassy. That is not my business. I only measure. Although it was quite a thick envelope.
No big ships in the bay. The embassy asked me to measure the bay again. I did. It is still the same size.
I measured the distance to your feet. Sorry. Habit. Two metres and a bit. The bit is the interesting part.
Oh. Hello again. Please don’t step on the string. That string is the coast, officially.
The embassies pay, I measure. What they do with the numbers is between them and the council, and the council votes in public. I find that very relaxing.
Then I have very accurate maps of a harbour that will never exist. It happens. My drawer is full of them. Some are quite beautiful.
I always look like this. My mother says I was born checking a measurement twice. Here it helps. On this island everything gets checked twice, even me.
Forty-two centimetres. Twice. Then the third one was forty-four. Either he is growing, or he walks faster when he is upset. I wrote a report. Nobody has asked for it.
So you found what was behind the waterfall. I knew it, dear. The sea gives things back to the patient ones.
Still got my chart, dear? Good. Follow the water, not the path. Paths are made by people in a hurry.
Back already, dear? I’ve just labelled the kettle. It was feeling left out.
Come aboard, dear, and mind the third step. It’s labelled, but nobody reads labels.
A ship’s log from a crew who swore they had never been here. The log said otherwise, in their own hand. Records outlive excuses, dear. That’s archaeology in one sentence.
I trust records about people. People change their minds, which is healthy. Records stop them changing the past, which is healthier.
This island keeps its agreements on a stone and in a Book. I wanted to see how a place lives that remembers everything. Politely, it turns out. Mostly.
I catalogue things, dear, I don’t believe in them. Item four hundred and twelve: one banana peel, folded, found on my deck. Origin unknown. Manners excellent.
The harbour law passed. Big ships, big waves. I’m building the sides higher.
Last day before the vote. Everyone’s in a hurry. The wood doesn’t care.
Morning. The wood is dry, the sea is calm, and nobody has asked me who I vote for. Yet.
Back again. The canoe is one plank further than yesterday. That’s fast, for a canoe.
You put three people in it. If they argue and it still floats, it’s ready.
It is the council. Ama taught me. It isn’t finished when one man says so. It’s finished when it holds everyone.
Behind the drums, at dusk. Big. Calm. He looked at the canoe like he was checking my work. Then he left. Took a banana. Fair.
Whoever cares about fish and music. I tell everyone the same, so nobody has to guess.
Your stone sits in the circle. It does not vote. It listens, like you did. That is why it stays.
The drums carried your truth across the hills. The hills don’t usually agree on anything. That evening they did.
You sat in the circle and listened. Rare, for a candidate. The others noticed. So did I.
You came back. The drums like that. Most people only come up here when there is bad news.
Welcome back. The drums are resting. A drummer rests between the beats. That’s half the music.
Oh, they tried. But every message goes out from three hills, and all three must match what the stone says. You’d have to bribe three drummers and a stone. The stone is very hard to talk to.
Then nothing is carried, and everyone comes down to the circle to find out why. Silence is the drums’ way of saying: not yet.
Anything that doesn’t break what we already agreed. Anyone can stand up and show the contradiction. If nobody can, it stands. It’s slow. Slow is how you know it’s real.
He likes the low drum. Some mornings the skin is warm, as if someone sat close all night, listening. He never plays. He only listens. A better audience than most.
A deep harbour. We say so openly. It is even in your Book. Ships need depth, and depth needs a vote. Ours is not a secret. It is merely expensive.
Then we wait for the next election. The North Wind is patient. Unfortunately, so is your Book. It remembers who promised and did not deliver.
Because there is nobody here who can sign it for us. No chief, no master key, only a council and a Book. Honestly, it is exhausting. Elsewhere one handshake is enough.
You did it, the road is law! I called my investors and for once they had nothing to say. Nothing! I think that means they’re happy. Come, have a smoothie, it’s on the house.

So the road passed. Wonderful. Only somebody else proposed it, and in the Book your name is next to my coins, not next to the road. My investors noticed before I did. About the road I’m happy. About you I’m still thinking.
The road is law. I keep saying it out loud, just to hear it. My guests will arrive like normal people now, in a minibus with the air conditioning on. Nobody has to cry.
Last day, and I still don’t see “A road round the island” in the Book. You have my coins. If it isn’t there tonight, I have to tell the island before the vote. I hate that part. I really do.

Last day, and we never did business, you and me. I respect that. I don’t like it, but I respect it. If you change your mind before the vote, the coins are right here, and the road still needs somebody.
You proposed it, I saw it in the Book. The council said no. Fine, that’s the council. You kept your word, and in my business that happens so rarely I don’t know what to do with my hands.
I hear Frost paid you. That’s okay, he pays more, I know. But he wants a harbour full of cruise ships, and I only want a little road. A road is very quiet, compared to a cruise ship. Think about it.
Running low, hm? Everybody is by now, campaigns are expensive. You know what I’m going to say, so I won’t say it. I’ll just sit here, next to the coins.

Ah, my partner! Your name is next to my coins in the Book, so we’re practically family now. The council tree is just down the hill. Propose “A road round the island” whenever you like. Before the election, ideally.
Did you go to the council tree yet? No? That’s fine. It’s fine. I’ll tell my investors you’re thinking about it. They love that. They love it when people think.
Ah, you came back! It’s the loungers, everybody comes back for the loungers. Same offer as before: the coins today, and you propose “A road round the island” before the election.
About the council tree. That was my investors, not me, I swear on my moustache. I told them you can’t buy a tree on this island. They didn’t listen. Now they’ve met Ama, and they’re very quiet.
Needed. Past tense! The road is law now, so now I need guests, which is a much nicer problem. You should see my booking calendar. Actually, don’t. Give it a week.

Right now there are two ways up to the resort: the jungle path, or my nephew’s wheelbarrow. The guests write about the wheelbarrow in their reviews. Every single one. With a road, the minibus stops at my gate.
I know, I know. Hana already came up here with a list. But my guests want quiet too, that’s what they pay me for. They just want to arrive at the quiet in a minibus.
Very well! Eleven rooms, and on a good night almost four of them are full. The pool is beautiful, you should see it with people in it. I saw it once. It was a Tuesday.
Because I make beautiful slides, and I say “synergy” a lot. They’ve never been here. If they came up the jungle path and saw the empty loungers… So, between us, please don’t invite them.

Me? I sell relaxing, I don’t do it. Every morning I join the guests for yoga, and every morning my phone rings in the middle of the tree pose. It’s always the investors. I have never once finished a tree.
Something big drinks from my pool at night. In the morning the water is lower and there’s a banana peel on a lounger, folded. Now I leave a towel out for him. Folded too. We have an understanding.
Everyone passes through here. Talk about what people care about; it counts double if you already passed a law for it.
The square belongs to everyone, and on Sunday night I count the ballots right here. Talk about what people care about; it counts double if you already passed a law for it.
Sit down, coffee first. Everything this island says is said here first, usually before it is true.
Sit down, coffee first. Everything this island says is said here first, usually before it is true.
Boats, gulls and a black cat that sometimes walks past twice. Nothing to do here but think. Tau Testnet Alpha is out there too: the Book on this island works a lot like its blocks.
Today’s lesson: a promise written where everyone can read it is worth more than one shouted on the radio. The children check the Book before they believe a rumour. Their parents are working on it.

We dive with Tau sensors. Every reading is signed the moment it is taken, so nobody can say the reef is fine when it is not. Or the other way round. Wetsuits are in the back, sizes small, medium and optimistic.
Coconuts in, everything out: oil, rope, soap, charcoal and once, by accident, a rather good jazz record. The machine is three bicycles and a church organ. Do not touch the organ.

We are only measuring. For whom? The embassies. For what? Something deep. We measure, others decide. That is the arrangement, and it pays by the metre.
The chart is yours now. Mind the waterfall: it is not as solid as it looks.
Not a pirate, dear. Marine archaeologist, retired. Everything the sea gives back ends up here, labelled: odd socks, a piano key, and a chart nobody can read.
My grandmother’s grandmother kept the island’s agreements on a stone, long before anyone wrote a Book. People think a record everyone can read is something new. It is the oldest thing we have.
A canoe is a promise kept by thirty planks. If one of them lies, the sea tells everyone. Same as your Book, really, only wetter.
Each mark is an agreement. Nobody ever chiselled one away, because everyone would see the scar. Your Book in the lighthouse is this stone, made of paper.
Before Radio Coco, the news went from hill to hill on these drums. They have one rule: they only carry what the stone confirms. That is why nobody ever bribed a drummer.
Here a decision stands when nobody in the circle can show that it contradicts what we already agreed. Not when the loudest agrees. Your chain does the same with its rules, I am told.
So you found it. The key on the old fort opens nothing; it never did. The real key was always this: everyone keeps a copy of what was agreed, so nobody can change it alone.

You saw him too? The old ones call him Agorzilla. He lives deep in the jungle and grows only in the ways the island votes for. Nobody has a clear photo, everybody has a theory, and the bananas keep disappearing.
Rico here, and I can smell it from the studio. The Coconut Works boiler went off like a drum solo. Noor says the road is the problem now, so expect everybody to care about roads today.
Morning, island. The pier is closed, the ferry is not coming, and three visitors are stranded on Lola’s floor. Whoever looks after visitors today will be remembered.
Big news, and it is not good. Someone tried to buy the council tree in the dark. Ama sat on it. The island wants quiet nights again, and everyone who took embassy money is being looked at.
Fish! Fish everywhere! The bay is silver, Sam is crying, and today the whole island cares about one thing. Whoever talks fish, wins ears.
Rain in the night, and the school roof is on the floor. Lessons under the tree. Parents are listening today, so whatever you say about the school, say it well.

I read the Book. You like an envelope, and you count. Good. There is a house on the hill nobody has bought since the old governor left. A hundred and fifty coins by election day and it is yours, whoever wins. Governors change. Houses stay.
Then not one coin to Rico. Every shift, every envelope, into the jar. I will keep the key dry.
Suit yourself. The hill will still be there. So will I.
I keep a list on the blackboard of laws this island needs and never gets. You passed one. Pass two more of your own and the children will learn your name for the right reasons, governor or not.
Good. Three laws. Not promises, laws. I erase one line for every one that passes.
Then I leave the list for the next candidate. It is a patient list.

Everyone wants to win. Boring. Nobody on this island has ever made someone else governor on purpose. The one at the bottom of every count: get them the chair, and I will tell everyone who really did it. That is the only kind of power that lasts.
A pact with them, your vote for their laws, your speeches where it helps them, and your mouth shut. I do the talking later.
Pity. It would have been the best story this café ever had.

Two days, and not one line in the Book I would be ashamed to read aloud. Rare. Win it like that, no rumours, no envelopes, no pact broken, and I will write the count so that it is read for fifty years.
Then it is simple. Say only what is true, promise only what you will do, and let them shout.
As you like. The Book takes every kind of governor. It only reads differently.
The Coconut Works boiler burst at dawn. Nobody hurt, coconut everywhere, and the road to the Works is a river of oil.
A storm closed the pier overnight. No ferry today, no visitors, and three stranded travellers sleep on the bar’s floor.
In the night Salado’s investors tried to buy the council tree. Ama sat on its roots until sunrise and the paper was never signed.
A record catch. The bay is full of fish and so is every doorstep, and Old Sam says the reef has not looked like this in forty years.
The school roof gave way in the night rain. Lessons under the council tree until further notice; Hana has borrowed every parasol on the island.
